A square root is the power <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, not 2.

Take the root first: the numbers stay small.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>16</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16^{-3/4}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>16</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{16^{3/4}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mroot><mn>16</mn><mn>4</mn></mroot><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\left(\sqrt[4]{16}\right)^3}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{2^3}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{8}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Power of a power multiplies: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^3)^2 = x^6</annotation></semantics></math>. Product adds: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msup><mo>⋅</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^6 \cdot x^{-4} = x^2</annotation></semantics></math>. Quotient subtracts: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x^2}{x} = x^{1} = x</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{6 - 4 - 1} = x^1</annotation></semantics></math>.

That comes from adding <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 + 2</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^3)^2</annotation></semantics></math>. A power of a power multiplies exponents: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^6</annotation></semantics></math>.

That forgets to divide by the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the denominator: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x^2}{x} = x</annotation></semantics></math>.

That squares the exponent, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^9</annotation></semantics></math>. A power of a power multiplies: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^3)^2 = x^{3 \cdot 2} = x^6</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: Split the fraction so each term is divided by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x^2}{x^{1/2}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \frac{1}{x^{1/2}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= x^{3/2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ x^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2 - 1/2} + x^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Both terms are divided by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, including the 1: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Dividing by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math> subtracts <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> from the exponent; it does not multiply it by 2.

The <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2</annotation></semantics></math> term is divided by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x}</annotation></semantics></math> too: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2 - 1/2} = x^{3/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2x)^3 = 8x^3</annotation></semantics></math>, so the expression is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{8x^3} = \frac{1}{8}x^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>. But <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x^{-3} = \frac{2}{x^3}</annotation></semantics></math>: the exponent there applies only to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, so it is 16 times too big.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x^{-3} = \frac{2}{x^3}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{8x^3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

A negative exponent on the whole base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2x)</annotation></semantics></math> is one over <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2x)^3</annotation></semantics></math>: equal.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2x)^3 = 2^3x^3 = 8x^3</annotation></semantics></math>: equal.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>8</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{1}{x^3} = \frac{1}{8x^3}</annotation></semantics></math>: equal.

why.correct: Same base, multiplied: add the exponents. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{5}{6}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}</annotation></semantics></math>.
That multiplies the exponents. Multiplying powers of the same base adds them.

Fractions add with a common denominator: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>≠</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} \ne \frac{2}{5}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That adds the denominators. Use a common denominator: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6}</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>4</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4}} = \frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 3</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mn>4</mn></msqrt><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4^{3/2} = (\sqrt{4})^3 = 8</annotation></semantics></math>. Total: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 + 8 = 11</annotation></semantics></math>.

Raise each factor to the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-2</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{-2}\left(x^{-1}\right)^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{4}x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{x^2}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^{-1})^{-2} = x^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

The 2 is raised to the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-2</annotation></semantics></math> as well: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, not 4.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^{-1})^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= x^{(-1)(-2)}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= x^2</annotation></semantics></math>, which goes in the numerator.

A negative exponent never makes the result negative; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: The exponent <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> applies to the whole sum: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x + 3)^{-1} = \frac{1}{x + 3}</annotation></semantics></math>. It cannot be split into separate terms.
options: One over the whole base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x + 3</annotation></semantics></math>.

Exponents do not distribute over a sum. Test <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 1</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, but <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The exponent <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> means reciprocal, not negative.

The exponent applies to the whole base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x + 3</annotation></semantics></math>, not only to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>27</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">27^{-1/3}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mroot><mn>27</mn><mn>3</mn></mroot></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{27}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4^{1/2} = 2</annotation></semantics></math>. The middle terms of a cube carry a factor 3: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3(2)^2h = 12h</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3(2)h^2 = 6h^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x - 9</annotation></semantics></math> is a difference of squares in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x - 9 = (\sqrt{x} - 3)(\sqrt{x} + 3)</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sqrt{x} - 3)^2</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x - 6\sqrt{x} + 9</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x - 9</annotation></semantics></math>. The factor that pairs with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x} - 3</annotation></semantics></math> is its conjugate.

That is the reciprocal: it is the simplified form of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\sqrt{x} - 3}{x - 9}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>25</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{1}{25}</annotation></semantics></math> is the value the expression approaches near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 5</annotation></semantics></math>, not the simplified expression.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan\frac{3\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\sin(3\pi/4)}{\cos(3\pi/4)}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\sqrt{2}/2}{-\sqrt{2}/2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -1</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}</annotation></semantics></math>. Adding <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> changes the sign of both sine and cosine, so the ratio is unchanged: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan(x + \pi) = \tan x</annotation></semantics></math>. The graph repeats every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, with asymptotes at odd multiples of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is where the first asymptote sits. One full repeat runs from one asymptote to the next, a distance of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.

The tangent graph repeats every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>: one full branch fits between neighboring asymptotes.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> is the period of sine and cosine. Tangent repeats twice as often.

Nothing stretches the graph of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan x</annotation></semantics></math>; it repeats every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.

The quadrant of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> does not matter here, because the identity uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^2 x</annotation></semantics></math>.

The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted left by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a shift left adds to the input: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos x = \sin\left(x + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin(x + \pi) = -\sin x</annotation></semantics></math>: a half turn flips the sign of sine.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \pi</annotation></semantics></math> this is 1, while <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\pi = -1</annotation></semantics></math>. The identity is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, with squares.

Cosine is sine shifted left by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1 = \cos 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: The log of a power: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\ln 2 = \ln 2^3 = \ln 8</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\ln 8} = 8</annotation></semantics></math>.

Log of a quotient, then log of a power: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln x^3 - \ln y</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 3\ln x - \ln y</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln\frac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln a^3 = 3\ln a</annotation></semantics></math>.
The log of a quotient is a difference of logs, not a quotient of logs.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(x^3) = 3\ln x</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(3x)</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(x^3) = 3\ln x</annotation></semantics></math>; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\ln x)^3</annotation></semantics></math> is something else.

why.correct: Take <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln</annotation></semantics></math> of both sides: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x = \ln 9</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\ln 9}{2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{2\ln 3}{2}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \ln 3</annotation></semantics></math>.

Exponentiate both sides: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x + 2 = e^1 = e</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.718</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = e - 2 \approx 0.718</annotation></semantics></math>. Check: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x + 2 = e > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, inside the domain.

A logarithm needs a positive input: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 - x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x < 4</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 - x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

For <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > 4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 - x</annotation></semantics></math> is negative.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 4</annotation></semantics></math> the input is 0, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 0</annotation></semantics></math> is not defined.

The input of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4 - x</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">12 = 3 \cdot 4</annotation></semantics></math>, and the log of a product is the sum of the logs.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(3 \cdot 4)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Logs turn products into sums, not products.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 10 + \ln 2 = \ln 20</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\ln 6 = \ln 36</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^x}</annotation></semantics></math>: positive for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, equal to 1 at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, and smaller as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> grows. It is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = e^x</annotation></semantics></math> reflected over the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-axis.
options: Positive, through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>, decreasing.
That describes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = e^x</annotation></semantics></math>.

That describes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = -e^x</annotation></semantics></math>; the minus here is in the exponent.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-1} \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>; an exponential is never 0.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>500</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>0.04</mn><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500e^{0.04t}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>800</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 800</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">⇒</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>0.04</mn><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Rightarrow e^{0.04t}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1.6</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">⇒</mo><mn>0.04</mn><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Rightarrow 0.04t</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1.6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \ln 1.6</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">⇒</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Rightarrow t</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1.6</mn></mrow><mn>0.04</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\ln 1.6}{0.04}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>11.750</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 11.750</annotation></semantics></math> years.

The log of a power: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(x^p) = p\ln x</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: The exponent comes out front as a multiplier.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\ln x)^2</annotation></semantics></math> squares the log, a different function: at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = e</annotation></semantics></math> it is 1, but <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(e^2) = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 2 + \ln x = \ln(2x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Adding 2 is not the same as multiplying by 2.

why.correct: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 5 + \ln 2 = \ln 10</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\ln 10} = 10</annotation></semantics></math>. (Or: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\ln 5}e^{\ln 2} = 5 \cdot 2</annotation></semantics></math>.)

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\ln x = \ln x^{-1} = \ln\frac{1}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-\ln x} = \frac{1}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\ln(1/x)} = \frac{1}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The minus sign becomes an exponent of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>, not a negative output; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> to any power is positive.
That ignores the minus sign.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-\ln x}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{e^{\ln x}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\ln x}</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: Logs turn products into sums. Test the others with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = y = e</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>1.69</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(2e) \approx 1.69</annotation></semantics></math>, not 2; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>1</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1} = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, but <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 0</annotation></semantics></math> is undefined; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1^2 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>, not 2.
options: The log of a product is a sum of logs.

At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = y = e</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>1.69</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(2e) \approx 1.69</annotation></semantics></math>, but <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln e + \ln e = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

There is no rule for a quotient of logs; at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = y</annotation></semantics></math> the right side is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(1) = 5</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(5) = 1</annotation></semantics></math>. The superscript <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> means "inverse", not "reciprocal".

Check: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(0) = -\frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{0}{-7/3} = 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

Solve <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = y^3 + 2</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^3 = x - 2</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mroot><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></mroot></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = \sqrt[3]{x - 2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">[</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arcsin\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Arccosine gives an angle in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0, \pi]</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Arctangent gives an angle in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -1</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Inside first: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arcsin\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}</annotation></semantics></math>. The two functions do not cancel here, because <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>6</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{5\pi}{6}</annotation></semantics></math> is outside arcsine's range.

An inverse must send each output back to one input. Since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(2) = f(-2)</annotation></semantics></math>, the horizontal line <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 4</annotation></semantics></math> meets the graph twice. On <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math> the function is one-to-one, and its inverse is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: It fails the horizontal line test on all of its domain.

On <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 0</annotation></semantics></math> it has the inverse <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x}</annotation></semantics></math>; nonnegative outputs are fine.
Many curves have inverses; being one-to-one is what matters.
<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2</annotation></semantics></math> is defined for every real number.

why.correct: Reflecting across <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = x</annotation></semantics></math> swaps coordinates, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2, 7)</annotation></semantics></math> becomes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(7, 2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and swaps rise and run, so slope 4 becomes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Swap the point and flip the slope.
The reflection swaps rise and run, so the slope flips to its reciprocal.
The point must be swapped too.

Reflection across <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = x</annotation></semantics></math> swaps coordinates; it does not negate them.

why.correct: A <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> written on a function name means the inverse function: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^{-1} x = \arcsin x</annotation></semantics></math>. (Compare <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^2 x = (\sin x)^2</annotation></semantics></math>; the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> is the exception.)
options: The inverse of sine on its restricted domain.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>csc</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\csc x</annotation></semantics></math>; it is written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sin x)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
An inverse is not a negative.

That would be written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)</annotation></semantics></math>: the sine of a reciprocal input. The <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math> on the name <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin</annotation></semantics></math> means the inverse function.

why.correct: A function that only increases (or only decreases) is one-to-one. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = 2x - 5</annotation></semantics></math> rises steadily, so every horizontal line meets its graph once, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x + 5}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(3) = f(-3) = 4</annotation></semantics></math>: two inputs share an output, so it fails the horizontal line test.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|2| = |-2| = 2</annotation></semantics></math>, so two inputs share an output.

Sine repeats: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin 0 = \sin\pi = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. It needs a restricted domain before it has an inverse.
A line with nonzero slope only increases or only decreases, so each output comes from exactly one input.

why.correct: A function and its inverse undo each other: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(f(x)) = x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(f^{-1}(x)) = x</annotation></semantics></math>. So the sum is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8 + (-2) = 6</annotation></semantics></math>, whatever <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is.

The outputs of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos x</annotation></semantics></math> are the angles with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0 \le \theta \le \pi</annotation></semantics></math>, so a negative angle such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is outside the range. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos 1 = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, so 0 is an output.

Arccosine returns angles from 0 to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, so no output is negative. (Arcsine and arctangent can return <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\frac{\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.)

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, so this is an output.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos(-1) = \pi</annotation></semantics></math>, so this is an output.

why.correct: The ladder, wall and ground form a right triangle with hypotenuse 13: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>13</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5^2 + y^2 = 13^2</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>144</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^2 = 144</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 12</annotation></semantics></math> feet.

The water forms a smaller cone similar to the tank, so the ratio of radius to depth is the same: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{r}{h} = \frac{6}{9} = \frac{2}{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: Similar triangles: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{r}{h} = \frac{6}{9}</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is depth over radius; the ratio is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{r}{h} = \frac{6}{9}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Similar shapes scale by a factor; they do not differ by a constant.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> are legs of the side-view triangle, not a radius and a slant length of 6.

Right: square, add and use <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1</annotation></semantics></math>.

Dividing gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>y</mi><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{y}{x} = \tan t</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is the parameter, not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>: the path is not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 3\tan x</annotation></semantics></math>. Squaring and adding removes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.

With <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2(2) + 1 = 5</annotation></semantics></math>. Subtract by components: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">⟨</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\langle 2 - (-1), 1 - 5 \right\rangle</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">⟨</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \left\langle 3, -4 \right\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>. Its magnitude is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>25</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2 + y^2 = 25</annotation></semantics></math>, a circle of radius 5. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 0</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(5, 0)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 5)</annotation></semantics></math>: from the right side to the top is counterclockwise. One turn takes <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0 \le t \le 6\pi</annotation></semantics></math> is three turns.

Here the interval has length <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, which is three turns.

Radius 5, from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(5, 0)</annotation></semantics></math> up to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 5)</annotation></semantics></math> first, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6\pi}{2\pi} = 3</annotation></semantics></math> turns.

From <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(5, 0)</annotation></semantics></math> at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 0</annotation></semantics></math> the point goes to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 5)</annotation></semantics></math> at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is counterclockwise.

A longer <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-interval repeats the same circle; it does not change the radius, which is 5.
